GPU memory in cuplyr

Source: vignettes/memory.Rmd
memory.Rmd

Introduction

Every process on a GPU shares its memory: your R session, other R sessions, a Python notebook, the desktop. cuplyr allocates many short-lived columns while it runs a pipeline. How it asks the driver for that memory decides how fast each call is, how much of the card cuplyr keeps after you drop a table, and how much is left for other processes.

This article covers the three ways cuplyr can allocate, how to switch between them, how to read what cuplyr holds, when memory is freed, and how to choose. It ends with numbers from one machine.

library(cuplyr)
library(dplyr)

The three resources

When it loads, cuplyr installs one RMM memory resource. Every GPU allocation in the R process goes through it.

Resource What it is Speed per allocation Memory after you drop a table Sharing the card
"async" (default) CUDA’s stream-ordered allocator (cudaMallocAsync) Fast, same as the pool Cached for reuse until gpu_gc() returns it, or returned by CUDA with the opt-in cuplyr.release_threshold Good, gpu_gc() hands back what you dropped
"pool" RMM’s pool, one big reservation split into columns Fast Kept until the R session ends, the pool never shrinks Poor, the card stays as full as your peak
"cuda" No resource, a plain cudaMalloc/cudaFree per column Slowest Returned to the device when R collects the table Good, but every allocation pays the driver

With async, cuplyr reserves cuplyr.pool_initial bytes at load so the first calls need no driver allocation. The default is a quarter of free device memory, at most 1 GiB. The async pool then grows when a pipeline needs more and keeps what it grew to for the next call, which is why it is as fast as the pool. Unlike the pool it can give memory back. gpu_gc() synchronises the device and returns everything the async pool holds unused, so a pipeline that briefly needed 6 GB doesn’t hold 6 GB for the rest of the session.

Automatic release

To get memory back without calling gpu_gc(), set cuplyr.release_threshold in bytes. At every GPU synchronisation, CUDA then returns unused memory until the pool’s whole reservation is at or below the threshold. The reservation includes the tables you hold and results R hasn’t collected yet. So while your session holds more than the threshold, nothing freed stays cached, and every allocation goes to the driver at about the speed of plain cudaMalloc. A threshold of 0 keeps nothing. libcudf synchronises inside many calls, not only in collect(), print() and gpu_sync(), so a release can happen in the middle of a pipeline. The table at the end shows the cost.

Switching resources

cuplyr picks the resource when the package loads, one per R process. Set the option before library(cuplyr), and restart R to change it.

What Option Environment variable
Kind of resource: "async" (default), "pool", or "cuda"/"none" for no resource cuplyr.memory_resource CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE
Turn the resource off ("cuda"): FALSE, "0", "false", "no", "off" cuplyr.memory_pool CUPLYR_MEMORY_POOL
How much the resource reserves at load, in bytes (not a limit) cuplyr.pool_initial CUPLYR_POOL_INITIAL
Async only: release unused memory automatically while the whole reservation is above this many bytes cuplyr.release_threshold CUPLYR_RELEASE_THRESHOLD

An option wins over its environment variable. Case and surrounding spaces don’t matter. cuplyr_options() shows the values as set now, which take effect at the next load, not the ones this session’s resource was installed with. ?"cuplyr-options" documents them all.

cuplyr warns about invalid values and falls back:

  • An unknown kind, say "managed", gives "async". If cuplyr.memory_pool turns the resource off, the kind is ignored and no resource is used.
  • A cuplyr.release_threshold of NA or "" counts as unset, so the environment variable decides. Any other value that isn’t a non-negative number means no automatic release. "pool" and "cuda" ignore the threshold.
  • If the GPU or driver doesn’t support cudaMallocAsync and async was only the default, cuplyr installs "pool". If you asked for "async" by name, it installs no resource ("cuda").
# In a fresh R session, before loading cuplyr:
options(cuplyr.memory_resource = "pool")   # the pool instead of async
# or: options(cuplyr.memory_resource = "cuda")  # plain cudaMalloc; same as
#     options(cuplyr.memory_pool = FALSE)
# or: options(cuplyr.release_threshold = 0)      # async: keep nothing cached
library(cuplyr)

From a shell, CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE=pool Rscript script.R does the same. cuplyr.pool_initial = 0 only skips the reservation at load. The pool still grows and caches as it needs.

Reading the numbers

gpu_memory_state() reports the device and what cuplyr’s resource holds.

st <- gpu_memory_state()
st$resource
#> [1] "async"
c(free = st$free_bytes, pool = st$pool_bytes, in_use = st$pool_used_bytes)
#>        free        pool      in_use 
#> 11604656128    33554432     1138378
  • free_bytes, used_bytes and total_bytes cover the whole device, every process, as nvidia-smi shows. used_bytes includes memory the resource keeps for reuse, so dropping a table doesn’t lower it until the memory goes back. Under "pool" that never happens. Under "async" it happens after gpu_gc() or an automatic release.
  • pool_bytes is what cuplyr’s resource holds from the device.
  • pool_used_bytes is what cuplyr uses for live columns and scratch space. It rises when you create a table and falls when R collects it.
  • Under "cuda" there is no resource, so pool_bytes and pool_used_bytes are NA and free_bytes tells the whole story.

To see how big your tables are, read pool_used_bytes. To see how much of the card you take from others, read pool_bytes or free_bytes.

gpu_df <- tbl_gpu(data.frame(x = runif(1e6)), lazy = FALSE)
gpu_memory_usage(gpu_df)  # estimate from dimensions and types
#> [1] 8125000
gpu_memory_state()$pool_used_bytes
#> [1] 9138378

gpu_memory_usage() estimates a table’s size from its row count and column types without touching the device. Tables that share columns, such as a select() of another table, overlap in this estimate.

When is memory freed?

  1. A call frees its own intermediates. A lazy table, the default, holds nothing for its pending steps. An eager verb, compute(), collect() or bind_rows() frees the temporary tables its steps built when it returns.
  2. Tables you hold live until R’s garbage collector runs. After rm(gpu_df) the memory is freed when R collects it. R doesn’t know about GPU memory pressure, so that can be late.
  3. gpu_gc() forces the collection. Under async it then returns all unused memory to the device. The next calls must grow the pool again, which costs the first call a few percent, so keep it out of timing loops. In the list it returns, freed_bytes is the drop in pool_used_bytes and released_bytes the drop in pool_bytes. released_bytes is 0 under "pool" and NA under "cuda". If the device is in a CUDA error state, gpu_gc() warns instead of failing.
  4. When a GPU step runs out of device memory, cuplyr runs gc() and gpu_gc(aggressive = FALSE) and retries the step once. A second failure raises an error of class cuplyr_error_gpu_oom.
rm(gpu_df)
res <- gpu_gc()
c(freed = res$freed_bytes, released = res$released_bytes)
#>    freed released 
#>  8002816        0

How to choose

  • Keep the default, async, unless you have a reason not to. It is as fast as the pool and gpu_gc() hands its memory back.
  • Use "pool" only when cuplyr is the card’s only user. It never gives memory back, not even after gpu_gc(). Released cuplyr versions up to 0.1.1 used no resource, which is "cuda".
  • Use "cuda" to debug memory, since device free memory is then exactly what you hold. Calls are slower.
  • If you share the card, stay on async and call gpu_gc() after a large job. If you can’t, set cuplyr.release_threshold above what your session holds while it works, counting live tables and uncollected results. Below that, every call allocates from the driver and runs at about the speed of "cuda".
  • No resource lets data bigger than the card fit. They only change how much is held on the side.

Measured on this machine

Measured on 2026-10-23 with cuplyr 0.1.1.9000 on an RTX 5070 (12 GB). Each number is the median of 3 fresh R processes per configuration. The table is static and nothing is timed when this vignette builds.

The columns are async as shipped, async with cuplyr.release_threshold = 0, pool, and cuda. Per-call time is the median over batches of calls after warm-up, with a GPU synchronisation at the end of each batch.

  • Small eager mutate: mutate(z = x * 2 + y) on an eager 1000-row table.
  • 1e6-row lazy pipeline: filter(), mutate(), group_by(), summarise() and collect() on a lazy 1e6-row table.
  • 25M-row workflow: the README benchmark (filter(), mutate(), group_by(), summarise(), collect()) on a lazy table of 25 million rows and 6 columns, about 1 GB on the GPU.

Held memory is extra device memory in use compared with a starting point taken after gpu_gc() and before the table exists. “After gc + sync” means after dropping the table, running gc() and synchronising. The last row is pool_bytes after the 1 GB run’s gpu_gc().

Measurement async async, release_threshold = 0 pool cuda
Small eager mutate (ms per call) 0.85 0.86 0.84 0.87
1e6-row lazy pipeline (ms per call) 3.3 3.5 3.3 4.1
25M-row workflow (ms per call) 14.3 19.0 14.3 18.0
1 GB table dropped, extra memory held after gc + sync (GB) 1.01 0.00 0.00 0.00
1 GB table, after gpu_gc() (GB) 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.00
3 GB table dropped, extra memory held after gc + sync (GB) 3.02 0.00 4.29 0.00
3 GB table, after gpu_gc() (GB) 0.00 0.00 4.29 0.00
Held by the resource after gpu_gc(), 1 GB run (GB) 0.00 0.00 4.29 n/a (no resource)
  • Default async and pool run at the same speed. Plain cuda is slower at 1e6 rows (4.1 ms) and about 25% slower on the 25M-row workflow (18.0 ms).
  • async with release_threshold = 0 keeps nothing after a synchronisation, but every call allocates from the driver again. The 25M-row workflow takes 19.0 ms, about a third slower than the default.
  • Default async keeps a dropped table cached (1.01 and 3.02 GB) until gpu_gc() returns all of it.
  • pool ran its measurements in order in one process, and the 25M-row workflow had already grown the pool to 4.29 GB. The 1 GB table fit inside that. The 3 GB table grew the pool by another 4.29 GB, since it grows in large steps, and the pool kept it even after gpu_gc().
  • cuda gets memory back as soon as R collects the table.

To repeat the measurement, run the code below once per configuration, each in a fresh session started with CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE=async, CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE=async CUPLYR_RELEASE_THRESHOLD=0, CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE=pool, or CUPLYR_MEMORY_POOL=0, and take the median of a few runs.

library(cuplyr)
library(dplyr)

# Median seconds per call over `samples` batches of `reps` calls.
per_call <- function(fn, reps, samples = 15, warmup = 5) {
  for (i in seq_len(warmup)) fn()
  gpu_sync()
  t <- vapply(seq_len(samples), function(i) {
    gc(verbose = FALSE)
    t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
    for (j in seq_len(reps)) fn()
    gpu_sync()
    (proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0) / reps
  }, numeric(1))
  median(t)
}

small <- tbl_gpu(data.frame(x = runif(1000), y = runif(1000)), lazy = FALSE)
1e3 * per_call(function() mutate(small, z = x * 2 + y), reps = 200)

big <- data.frame(x = runif(1e6), y = runif(1e6), k = sample.int(100L, 1e6, TRUE))
lz <- tbl_gpu(big, lazy = TRUE)
1e3 * per_call(function() {
  lz |> filter(x > 0.1) |> mutate(z = x * y) |>
    group_by(k) |> summarise(s = sum(z)) |> collect()
}, reps = 10)
rm(small, lz, big)

# README-scale workflow: 25M rows x 6 columns (about 1 GB on the GPU).
n <- 25e6
taxi <- data.frame(
  VendorID = sample(1:4, n, replace = TRUE),
  payment_type = sample(1:5, n, replace = TRUE),
  fare_amount = pmax(2.5, rnorm(n, mean = 13, sd = 10)),
  tip_amount = pmax(0, rnorm(n, mean = 2.5, sd = 3)),
  tolls_amount = runif(n, 0, 15),
  trip_distance = pmax(0.1, rexp(n, rate = 0.3)))
tg <- tbl_gpu(taxi, lazy = TRUE)
rm(taxi); gc()
1e3 * per_call(function() {
  tg |> filter(fare_amount > 0, trip_distance > 0) |>
    mutate(fare_per_mile = fare_amount / trip_distance) |>
    group_by(VendorID, payment_type) |>
    summarise(avg_fare_per_mile = mean(fare_per_mile),
              avg_tip = mean(tip_amount), .groups = "drop") |>
    collect()
}, reps = 3, samples = 9, warmup = 2)
rm(tg)

# Held memory for a table of n doubles (1.25e8 = 1 GB, 3.75e8 = 3 GB).
held <- function(n) {
  host <- data.frame(a = runif(n))
  gpu_gc()
  free0 <- gpu_memory_state()$free_bytes   # the starting point
  g <- tbl_gpu(host, lazy = FALSE)
  gpu_sync()
  rm(g); gc(); gc()
  gpu_sync()
  after_gc_sync <- free0 - gpu_memory_state()$free_bytes
  gpu_gc()
  s <- gpu_memory_state()
  after_gpu_gc <- free0 - s$free_bytes
  c(after_gc_sync = after_gc_sync, after_gpu_gc = after_gpu_gc,
    pool_bytes = s$pool_bytes) / 1e9
}
held(1.25e8)
held(3.75e8)
